content.body:
Glenohumeral osteoarthritis (GHOA) is degenerative disease of the shoulder's ball-and-socket joint — progressive loss of articular cartilage, subchondral bone change, osteophyte formation and capsular contracture, producing pain, stiffness and loss of function.

It is the second most common diagnosis in patients presenting with atraumatic shoulder pain, after rotator cuff disease. Radiographic prevalence in middle-aged and older adults runs at 16–20%.
The shoulder has three joints that can degenerate, and they behave completely differently:

rows: Deep, diffuse pain · global stiffness · crepitus · loss of rotation
Point tenderness over the AC joint · pain on cross-body adduction · often asymptomatic on imaging
Crepitus and snapping, rarely a primary degenerative problem

content.body: AC joint OA is far more common than glenohumeral OA and very often incidental. Writing "shoulder OA" in a letter without specifying the joint tells the next clinician nothing — and risks a patient being told they have arthritis in a joint that is not the one hurting.

You will see both. "Osteoarthrosis" was used deliberately to emphasise that this was degeneration without inflammation — the "-osis" ending chosen for the same reason the tendon literature moved from tendinitis to tendinosis.

That reasoning no longer holds. GHOA involves genuine synovial inflammation: synovitis with elevated IL-1 and reduced IL-1 receptor antagonist, protease-driven chondral breakdown, and signalling between inflammatory cells, chondrocytes and subchondral bone.

content.label: Key Takeaway
content.text: Use "osteoarthritis." The inflammatory component is real, and it is part of why corticosteroid injection does anything at all.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Worth noticing that this is the opposite correction to the one made in tendinopathy. There, we removed "-itis" because the inflammation wasn't there. Here, we keep it because it is. The lesson is the same either way: name the condition after the mechanism you can actually demonstrate.
Why the shoulder is not just a small hip

content.body:
This is the organising idea of the whole chapter. GHOA is far less common than hip or knee OA, and it does not behave the same way.

1. It is not weight-bearing. The shoulder does not fail under axial load the way a hip does. Obesity, a dominant mechanical risk factor at the knee, is not associated with increased early postoperative complications in shoulder arthroplasty — and the AAOS rates that as strong evidence.

2. The wear is eccentric, not concentric. Hips and knees tend to wear symmetrically. The shoulder characteristically wears posteriorly, with the humeral head subluxing backwards and eroding the posterior glenoid. That asymmetry is why the Walch classification exists and why glenoid version dominates surgical planning.

3. The rotator cuff has no equivalent at the hip or knee. A soft-tissue envelope actively centres this joint. When it fails, the mechanics change completely — and you get a different disease, not a worse one.

4. Scapular and acromial morphology contribute, including premorbid retroversion and acromial dysplasia — anatomical factors with no real parallel in the lower limb.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: A limitation worth knowing: most of what we believe about GHOA pathobiology is extrapolated from knee osteoarthritis. The 2025 review from the Arthritis Foundation/AOSSM Think Tank states explicitly that the post-traumatic and post-surgical pathways identified in the knee "require future validation in studies of GHOA." We are reasoning by analogy more than we usually admit.

content.body: (From 209 consecutive GHOA patients in a community musculoskeletal practice.)

rows: Recurrent dislocation damages cartilage and labrum — dislocation arthropathy
Over-tightened anterior repair drives the head posteriorly — capsulorrhaphy arthropathy
Intra-articular proximal humeral fracture, chondral injury
Throwing athletes, overhead work — association, not established cause

content.text: The finding that undermines the "wear and tear" story

content.body: Primary GHOA affects the dominant and non-dominant arm at nearly the same rate:

If this were a disease of cumulative use, the dominant arm should dominate. It does not.

The study authors' conclusion is that anatomical and systemic factors matter more than overuse — and the risk factor profile supports it. Patients with primary GHOA in that series had a mean BMI of 31.0, with 57.2% hypertensive and 48.7% hyperlipidaemic; the 2025 review adds smoking to the list.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: This is a systemic and anatomical disease more than a mechanical one. That changes what you say to patients. The person who asks "is this because of my job?" usually expects to be told yes, and the honest answer is that in primary GHOA the evidence points more toward age, anatomy and metabolic factors than toward how they used the arm.

content.body: It also means the other shoulder deserves attention — bilateral involvement is over a quarter of cases.

content.text: Cuff tear arthropathy — a different disease, not a worse one

rows: Loss of the fulcrum → superior migration → the head articulates with the acromion

content.body: In CTA the joint surface fails because the cuff did. The humeral head rides up, the undersurface of the acromion becomes a false socket — acetabularisation — and the joint is destroyed from above rather than from within.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Separate these two before planning anything. They look alike in clinic: an older patient with a painful, stiff, crepitant shoulder. But cuff status determines the examination you emphasise, the imaging you order, the operation offered, the rehabilitation protocol, and what you can honestly promise about rotation afterwards.

content.body: The lag signs and the acromiohumeral interval are what separate them — one from your hands, one from a plain film. Neither costs anything.

content.text: What this condition actually costs patients

content.body:
• 16% of adults experience disabling shoulder pain on a daily basis
  • Among those with atraumatic shoulder pain, GHOA is second only to rotator cuff disease
  • In one community practice series, 24.3% of patients diagnosed with GHOA had surgery within two years

That last figure is worth holding on to. A quarter progressed to arthroplasty within 24 months of diagnosis — so while this is a slowly progressive condition, a meaningful proportion of the people you diagnose are on a surgical pathway already.

The 2025 Think Tank review named five gaps, and two sit directly in PM&R's territory:

  1. The role of novel pharmacological agents
  2. The natural history of traumatic instability and its relationship to GHOA
  3. Which cuff tears predictably progress to secondary GHOA
  4. The efficacy of physical therapy for GHOA
  5. Why reverse and anatomic arthroplasty differ in perioperative morbidity and outcome

Also unresolved: whether the muscle imbalances seen in GHOA cause glenoid wear or result from it.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: Number 4 deserves emphasis, because it shapes the treatment chapter. The efficacy of physical therapy in glenohumeral OA is listed as an open question by the field's own consensus review — and the physiotherapy clinical practice guideline could only issue expert-opinion statements for non-operative care. That is not a reason to withhold rehabilitation. It is a reason not to claim more for it than we can support.

content.body: In a UK primary care population aged 45+ referred for shoulder radiographs, 21.2% had radiographic glenohumeral OA.
No meaningful sex difference overall (21.4% female, 21.0% male).

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: Two caveats on that figure. These were patients referred because they had shoulder pain, so this is not general-population prevalence. And radiographic change is not the same as symptomatic disease — the authors themselves caution that the changes may not be the cause of the pain. As with every joint, the X-ray and the patient are two different things.
How GHOA patients differ from cuff disease patients

content.body: In a community musculoskeletal practice over nine months, 984 patients were diagnosed with rotator cuff disorders and 209 with GHOA.

That twelve-year age gap is clinically useful: GHOA is a disease of a meaningfully older population than cuff disease. Women made up 54% of primary GHOA cases and were older than the men (72.9 vs 66.1 years).

rows: The dominant factor. Prevalence roughly sevenfold higher at 80 than at 45
Recurrent dislocation, and over-tightened stabilisation surgery
Proximal humeral fracture, especially intra-articular; chondral injury
Premorbid glenoid retroversion, acromial dysplasia, low critical shoulder angle
Overhead work, throwing, weightlifting — associations, not established causes

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Note what sits high on that list: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, raised BMI and smoking. Combined with the arm-dominance finding from section 1, the picture is of a condition with a metabolic and anatomical profile, not a straightforward overuse injury. Screening and addressing cardiovascular risk in these patients is defensible on general grounds — and smoking is one of only two modifiable predictors of a worse surgical outcome.

content.body: Three things matter for understanding OA here.

content.text: The socket is shallow, and its orientation matters

content.body:
The glenoid is small and shallow — normally retroverted a few degrees and slightly inclined superiorly. In OA, that geometry changes, and how it changes determines the operation.

Posterior erosion is the characteristic pattern. The humeral head drifts posteriorly, grinds away the back of the glenoid, and creates a biconcave socket — the Walch B2 glenoid. Restoring version is the central technical challenge of shoulder arthroplasty.

content.text: The rotator cuff is the joint's stabiliser

content.body:
The cuff compresses the head into the glenoid and keeps the centre of rotation fixed. When it fails, the deltoid drags the head superiorly, and the acromiohumeral interval narrows.

This is why cuff integrity decides the operation. An intact cuff allows an anatomic replacement. A deficient cuff requires a reverse replacement, which moves the centre of rotation and lets the deltoid elevate the arm without a cuff.

The angle between the glenoid plane and a line to the inferolateral acromion. A low CSA is associated with glenohumeral OA; a high CSA with cuff disease.

It is one of the few radiographic measurements the physiotherapy guideline identifies as predictive — alongside age — for differentiating GHOA.

The sequence is familiar from other joints, with shoulder-specific features.

1. Cartilage degradation. Matrix metalloproteinase activity exceeds repair. Proteoglycan is lost, collagen architecture degrades, and the surface fibrillates and thins.

2. Synovial inflammation. Synovitis with elevated IL-1 and reduced IL-1 receptor antagonist. Wnt and TGF-β signalling are implicated in cartilage health. This is the component that justifies the "-itis" and explains why corticosteroid helps.

3. Subchondral bone response. Sclerosis, cyst formation, and osteophytes — classically an inferior humeral head osteophyte, the "goat's beard," which is often the earliest radiographic sign.

4. Asymmetric wear. Unlike the hip, the shoulder tends to wear posteriorly. The head subluxes posteriorly, the posterior glenoid erodes, retroversion increases, and the socket becomes biconcave. This is progressive — one series found 79% of B1 glenoids progressed to B2 over about six years.

5. Capsular contracture. The anterior capsule and subscapularis shorten. This is why GHOA patients are stiff, not just sore — and why loss of external rotation is such a characteristic finding.

6. Synovitis and loose bodies. Secondary inflammation contributes pain; cartilage and osteophyte fragments can produce mechanical symptoms.

content.label: Memory aid
content.text: GHOA wears backwards and tightens forwards. Posterior erosion, anterior contracture. That combination explains the examination findings and the surgical difficulty in one phrase.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: Glenoid wear is described as multifactorial — muscle imbalance, premorbid retroversion and acromial dysplasia all contribute. Whether muscle imbalance causes glenoid wear or results from it remains unresolved, which matters because the first would make it a rehabilitation target and the second would not.

content.body: Also worth knowing: markers such as CTX-II remain elevated for weeks after surgery, so surgery itself acts as a secondary inflammatory insult to an already inflamed joint.
Three systems matter. Each answers a different question.
The simplest radiographic grading, based on inferior osteophyte size:

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: Radiographic severity does not predict who needs further treatment. In a prospective injection study, Samilson-Prieto grade did not predict the need for secondary intervention. Grade the X-ray, but treat the patient.
Walch — what shape is the glenoid, and what operation does it need?

content.body: The classification that drives surgical planning. Based originally on 2D axial CT, revised in 2016 using 3D CT.

rows: Head centred, major erosion (a tangent line to the native glenoid cuts through the humeral head)
Posterior subluxation, posterior joint narrowing, sclerosis and osteophytes — no significant erosion
Posterior subluxation with a biconcave glenoid from posterior erosion
Uniconcave glenoid from posterior erosion, with ≥15° retroversion and/or ≥70% posterior subluxation
Retroversion >25° not caused by erosion — dysplastic

content.body: The 2016 modification matters. The original classification had poor reliability (interobserver κ 0.391). Adding B3 and D, redefining A2 and C, and moving to 3D CT raised agreement to κ 0.703, and intraobserver agreement to 0.882.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: The B2 glenoid is the one to know. Biconcave, posteriorly eroded, posteriorly subluxed — and the central technical problem in shoulder arthroplasty. Place a standard glenoid component on a retroverted biconcave socket and it loosens. B2 glenoids are also older and more retroverted than B1 (23.4° vs 14.9°), and B-type glenoids medialise over time. Under the original definitions, many B2 glenoids were mislabelled as C — and MRI is less accurate than CT at telling them apart.
Hamada — is this cuff tear arthropathy?

content.body: Based on the acromiohumeral interval (AHI):
A narrowed AHI on a plain film tells you the cuff has failed — before any soft tissue imaging is ordered.

• Gradual onset over months to years
  • Deep, aching shoulder pain, often poorly localised, sometimes referred to the deltoid insertion
  • Worse with activity, better with rest — initially
  • Night pain as disease advances
  • Progressive stiffness, which the patient may notice before the pain
  • Crepitus — grinding, clunking, catching
  • Pain on reaching, lifting, overhead use and rotation

They do not say "I've lost external rotation." They say they cannot:

  • Reach a seatbelt or turn the steering wheel (external rotation)
  • Fasten a bra, reach a back pocket, manage toileting (internal rotation and extension)
  • Wash or dry their hair (abduction with external rotation)
  • Sleep on that side (the symptom that most often brings them in)

content.text: Features suggesting cuff tear arthropathy instead

content.body:
• Weakness disproportionate to pain
  • Pseudoparalysis — unable to elevate actively, but passive range preserved
  • Anterosuperior escape of the humeral head on attempted elevation
  • A long history of known cuff disease
Wasting of deltoid and the cuff from disuse. Asymmetry. Previous surgical scars — which change the differential entirely.

content.text: Range of motion — the core of the examination

content.body: Both active and passive range are restricted, because the block is mechanical. Measure with an inclinometer or goniometer, not by eye, and always compare sides.

rows: Characteristically lost first and worst — anterior capsular contracture
Reduced, measured by hand-behind-back spinal level

content.body: Crepitus through range is a useful positive finding — palpable and often audible grinding, which you rarely feel in frozen shoulder.
This is the commonest diagnostic confusion, and the examination alone will not always resolve it.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: The radiograph is what separates them. This is one of the few situations in shoulder medicine where imaging genuinely makes the diagnosis rather than confusing it — and it is precisely why a plain film is mandatory in a stiff shoulder before you label it frozen.

content.body:
Test the cuff specifically, because its integrity decides the operation:

  • Belly-press / lift-off — subscapularis
  • External rotation lag sign — infraspinatus
  • Hornblower's sign — teres minor
  • Drop arm — supraspinatus

A positive lag sign in a patient with OA changes the surgical plan from anatomic to reverse arthroplasty. That single finding is the highest-value thing in this examination.

• Cervical spine screen — referred pain, and C5 radiculopathy often has no neck pain
  • Acromioclavicular joint — frequently co-exists and is often the real pain source
  • Neurovascular examination
  • Functional assessment — what can they actually not do?

rows: Polyarticular, morning stiffness >1h, raised inflammatory markers
Risk factors (steroids, alcohol, sickle cell); early MRI change with preserved joint space
Point tenderness over the AC joint, positive cross-body adduction
Dermatomal pain, neurological signs, positive Spurling's
Night pain out of keeping, weight loss, lytic lesion on film

content.body:
Two views are essential:

  1. True AP (Grashey) — beam angled to the glenoid plane, showing the true joint space
  2. Axillary lateral — shows posterior subluxation, glenoid wear and posterior erosion

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: The axillary view is the one that gets omitted, and it is the one that carries the information. A standard AP will miss posterior subluxation entirely. It is also the view that detects a locked posterior dislocation — the classic missed diagnosis in a stiff shoulder.

content.body: What to look for: joint space narrowing · inferior humeral osteophyte (the "goat's beard") · subchondral sclerosis and cysts · posterior glenoid erosion · acromiohumeral interval (normal 7–14 mm; <7 mm suggests cuff failure) · loose bodies.

rows: Pre-operative planning. The reference standard for glenoid version, bone stock and Walch typing
When cuff integrity is in question, or for suspected AVN, or when the diagnosis is unclear

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: The AAOS guideline recommends axillary and true AP views for patients undergoing arthroplasty, with advanced imaging at clinician discretion (consensus). The physiotherapy guideline rates MRI as strong evidence for confirming GHOA — but notes it is less useful for ruling it out. Both agree the diagnosis is made from history, examination and plain films.

content.body: Not routine. Order inflammatory markers only if inflammatory or septic arthritis is in the differential.

Four principles, and the first is the one most often skipped.

1. Establish cuff status. Everything downstream depends on it. Intact cuff → anatomic pathway. Deficient cuff → reverse pathway.

2. Treat symptoms and function, not the radiograph. Radiographic severity does not predict who needs surgery, and it does not predict who responds to injection.

3. Non-surgical management first — but be honest about the evidence. It is worth trying. It does not reverse the disease, and the evidence base behind it is thin.

4. Arthroplasty is genuinely effective. Unlike many of the procedures in shoulder medicine, shoulder replacement for end-stage OA reliably relieves pain. The question is timing and implant choice, not whether it works.

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: This is the uncomfortable part of the chapter. The physiotherapy clinical practice guideline could issue only best practice statements — not graded recommendations — for non-operative management, because the evidence quality was rated insufficient. Specifically:

content.label: Guideline statement
content.text:
"Physical therapy may benefit patients who have not had TSA" — expert opinion
"No single physical therapist intervention is clearly superior to another" — expert opinion

content.body: That is an honest statement of where we are. Treat non-surgical management as reasonable, low-risk and worth offering — not as an evidence-based programme with a known effect size.

rows: Reduce provocative overhead and loaded positions. Not rest — modification
Capsular contracture is a major contributor to disability, and it is modifiable
Maintains the dynamic stabilisers and delays decompensation
Expectations, pacing, and what surgery can and cannot offer

content.body: Dose it by irritability, as in any painful shoulder: gentle and pain-free when highly irritable; progressively loaded as symptoms settle.

rows: First line. Topical NSAIDs are reasonable and lower-risk in older patients
AAOS: should not be used as routine long-term pain management
No recommendation for or against — insufficient evidence

content.body: The AAOS guideline makes no specific recommendation on NSAIDs or corticosteroid injection, which reflects the absence of trial data rather than a judgement against them.

content.text: Corticosteroid — the workhorse, with modest expectations

content.body: A prospective study of 30 shoulders with symptomatic GHOA, followed for 12 months after a single image-guided injection:

rows: Patients with worse baseline function gained significantly more
Did not predict need for further intervention

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Two useful messages. Expect roughly 3–4 months of meaningful functional benefit — tell the patient that number, because "it didn't last" is otherwise heard as failure. And do not withhold injection because the X-ray looks bad: severe radiographic disease responded as well as mild, and worse function predicted greater relief.

content.body:
Technique: use image guidance. The glenohumeral joint is deep and blind injection accuracy is poor.

Diabetes: as with any steroid injection, counsel glucose monitoring for 72 hours — peak rise is typically 24–72 hours, not 24.

content.label: AAOS recommendation
content.text: AAOS: STRONG evidence against. Hyaluronic acid shows no benefit for glenohumeral osteoarthritis.

content.body: This is one of the few strong negative recommendations in the guideline. It is also frequently offered. Know it.

content.text: PRP and stem cells — cannot be recommended

content.label: AAOS recommendation
content.text: AAOS: consensus — injectable biologics cannot be recommended.

content.body: Not "harmful," but unsupported. Patients will ask about these; the honest answer is that the evidence does not exist yet.
Acupuncture, dry needling, cannabis, CBD, cupping, TENS, capsaicin, glucosamine/chondroitin: no recommendation for or against — the evidence is insufficient either way.
Persistent pain and functional limitation despite reasonable non-surgical management, in a patient whose imaging matches their symptoms. There is no radiographic threshold that mandates surgery.

rows: Younger patients, focal disease, wanting to delay replacement
AAOS: non-prosthetic options may or may not provide short-term benefit (consensus)
AAOS: STRONG — anatomic TSA gives better function and pain relief than hemiarthroplasty
GHOA with an intact, functioning rotator cuff
Cuff-deficient shoulders, cuff tear arthropathy, severe glenoid bone loss, revision
Increasingly used beyond its original indications

content.text: Anatomic vs reverse in a cuff-intact shoulder

content.body: This is the live debate, and a 2026 systematic review addressed it directly.

rows: aTSA better — all ten studies reporting rotation favoured it
aTSA better in three studies — except in stiff shoulders (pre-op elevation ≤105°), where rTSA was better
No significant difference in any of nine studies
No difference in nine of ten studies
No difference in seven of nine studies

content.body: Authors' conclusions: comparable outcomes overall; aTSA preferable for mobile shoulders seeking better rotation; rTSA may be better for stiff osteoarthritic shoulders with an intact cuff; and age alone is not an indication for reverse.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: The practical translation for rehabilitation: an anatomic replacement should give better rotation; a reverse replacement will not. A patient who has had a reverse and cannot reach behind their back has not failed rehabilitation — that is the expected result of the implant, and it should have been said before surgery.

content.body:
• Do not use metal-backed cementless glenoid components (moderate evidence)
  • Pegged or keeled glenoids are both acceptable with a functioning cuff (strong)
  • Stemmed, stemless and resurfacing humeral components are all options (limited)
  • Subscapularis peel, lesser tuberosity osteotomy or tenotomy are all acceptable (moderate)

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Smoking and depression are the two modifiable predictors of a worse result. Both are within your scope before surgery, and neither is usually addressed. That is a genuine opportunity in pre-operative PM&R assessment.

content.body: This is where PM&R does most of its work in this condition.

rows: Sling + progressive ROM and strengthening after TSA improves outcomes and range
Sling in neutral rotation for pain management
Starting ROM may be delayed up to 4 weeks without harming outcomes
Post-operative physical therapy may benefit patient-rated function

content.label: Evidence note
content.text: That third row is important and counter-intuitive. Delaying range of motion by up to four weeks does not appear to harm patient-reported outcomes. Protocols vary enormously between surgeons, and the evidence does not strongly favour the aggressive end. When the operative note says wait — wait.
Anatomic TSA — the subscapularis governs everything

content.body: The subscapularis is taken down to access the joint and repaired at closure. Protecting that repair is the organising principle of the first six weeks.

rows: Sling continuously. Pendulums and gradual passive ROM only, per operative note. Active elbow, wrist and hand. No active shoulder ROM
Discontinue sling. Active-assisted → active ROM as permitted. Cane-assisted ER introduced within op-note limits
Full active and passive ROM maintained. Begin band and light-weight strengthening. ≤5 lb lifting
Graded return to work, recreation, sport

content.body:
Key precautions:

  • Limit external rotation per the operative note — this stresses the subscapularis repair
  • No reaching behind the back early — combined extension and internal rotation loads the repair
  • No active internal rotation until strengthening phase
  • Towel roll behind the elbow when supine for 4 weeks — prevents shoulder hyperextension stretching the subscapularis. The patient should be able to see their elbow.
  • No weight-bearing through the arm, no pushing up from a chair
  • No driving for 4 weeks or until out of the sling

content.text: Reverse TSA — the deltoid does the work, and dislocation is the risk

content.body: Different implant, different biomechanics, different precautions.

rows: Sling. Active elbow/wrist/hand from day 1. Pendulums from week 2. Tabletop activities only
Active-assisted → active. Ceiling punch, seated ER to neutral. No overhead reaching. Nothing heavier than a coffee cup
Deltoid isometrics and strengthening — anterior and middle deltoid. Lifting limit ~1 lb
Progress load gradually (≈2 lb). Functional activity per surgeon

content.body: Key precautions:

rows: Avoid extension with axial load (pushing up from a chair)
Avoid end-range internal rotation + adduction + extension (tucking in a shirt, toileting)
External rotation limits if subscapularis repaired

content.label: Pitfall
content.text: The combined position of internal rotation, adduction and extension is the dislocation position after reverse arthroplasty. It is exactly the movement used for toileting and tucking in a shirt. Teach it explicitly as a movement to avoid, with a practical workaround — because a patient told "avoid IR, adduction and extension" will not recognise it when they do it.

content.body: Rehabilitation emphasis differs fundamentally: in anatomic TSA you are protecting and then restoring the cuff. In reverse TSA the cuff is deficient and will not be restored — you train the deltoid. Avoid overtaxing it, particularly in osteopenic patients, where acromial and scapular spine stress fractures are a recognised complication.

content.text: Early versus delayed mobilisation after reverse TSA

content.body:
Randomised trials comparing early and delayed mobilisation found significant improvement in both groups and no significant long-term difference. A retrospective comparison of 0, 3 and 6 weeks of immobilisation found no differences in pain, outcomes, range of motion or satisfaction at one year.

The counterpoint: early mobilisation has been linked to acromion and scapular spine fractures, though the mechanism is debated.

Practical position: follow the surgeon's protocol. The evidence does not support overriding it in either direction, and the main argument for earlier motion is avoiding functional loss and deconditioning in frail older patients.
Patients ask this at the first post-operative visit. Give them numbers.
Work intensity is the strongest predictor. Suggested timelines:

By activity load after rTSA: 67% returned to low-load, 50% to high-load, 24% to medium-load activities. Highest return rates: swimming (84%), general fitness and golf (77% each).

Why people don't return: restricted motion (22%), fear of re-injury (21%), weakness (18%).

Suggested timelines: low-impact (swimming, cycling) 4–6 months; high-impact cautiously 6–8 months; contact sports not recommended, since high-impact activity may accelerate component wear.

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Fear of re-injury accounts for roughly as many non-returns as physical restriction. That is a rehabilitation problem, not a surgical one — and it is addressed by graded exposure and explicit permission, not by more strengthening.

content.body:
Non-surgically: GHOA is progressive. Non-surgical management controls symptoms; it does not alter the disease. Corticosteroid injection gives roughly 3–4 months of functional benefit and may give longer pain relief. In one community series, 24.3% proceeded to surgery within two years of diagnosis.

Surgically: shoulder arthroplasty is one of the more reliable operations in orthopaedics for pain relief. Reported reverse TSA survivorship reaches 91% at ten years.

What limits the result: smoking, depression, more comorbidities, and higher pre-operative function (less room to improve). Not obesity, and not sex.

Six things worth saying.

1. Name it plainly.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "The cartilage in your shoulder joint has worn, and the joint has stiffened up around it. It's the same process as arthritis in a hip or knee, just less common in the shoulder."

content.body: 2. The X-ray is not the patient.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "The X-ray tells us what the joint looks like. It doesn't tell us how much it should hurt — plenty of people have changes like this with very little pain, and the reverse is also true."

content.body: 3. It probably isn't your job.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "People usually assume this comes from wear and tear at work. For the common type, it affects the dominant and non-dominant arm at about the same rate — so it has more to do with age, your anatomy and general health than with how you've used the arm."

content.body: 4. Exercise is worth doing, and here's the honest reason.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "It won't rebuild the cartilage. What it does is keep the shoulder moving, keep the surrounding muscles strong, and delay the point where this limits you. That's a real benefit, but I don't want to oversell it."

content.body: 5. Injection buys months, not years.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "Expect about three to four months of meaningful benefit. If it works and then wears off, that's not a failure — that's what it does."

content.body: 6. Hyaluronic acid and PRP — say it clearly.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "There's good evidence that hyaluronic acid doesn't help in the shoulder, and not enough evidence to recommend PRP or stem cells. I'd rather tell you that than take your money."

content.body: 7. Surgery works, and the type matters.

content.label: Say it this way
content.text: "Shoulder replacement is genuinely effective for pain. Which type depends on your rotator cuff. If it's intact you get an anatomic replacement, which gives better rotation. If it's not, you get a reverse, which lets the shoulder lift again but won't give you full rotation back."

content.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content.text: Say the rotation limitation before the reverse replacement, not after. A patient who cannot reach behind their back at four months, and was never warned, will believe something went wrong. The same patient told in advance will accept it as the trade they agreed to.

content.body:
1. Specify the joint. "Shoulder arthritis" is not a diagnosis — AC joint OA is commoner and often incidental.
  2. Use "osteoarthritis," not "osteoarthrosis." The synovial inflammation is real, and it is why steroid works.
  3. GHOA is not a small hip. Not weight-bearing, wears eccentrically and posteriorly, and uniquely depends on the rotator cuff.
  4. ~73% is primary. It affects dominant and non-dominant arms almost equally — this is not simply a wear-and-tear disease.
  5. Radiographic prevalence reaches 37% by age 80–89 in people with shoulder pain — but the X-ray and the symptoms are separate questions.
  6. Establish cuff status first. It separates GHOA from cuff tear arthropathy and determines every subsequent decision.
  7. Two radiographs matter: true AP and axillary. The axillary view is the one that gets missed and the one that shows posterior subluxation.
  8. Learn the Walch B2 glenoid — biconcave, posteriorly eroded, and the central problem in arthroplasty planning.
  9. GHOA wears backwards and tightens forwards — posterior erosion, anterior contracture, loss of external rotation.
  10. Non-surgical management is reasonable but weakly evidenced. The efficacy of physical therapy is listed as an open question by the field's own consensus review.
  11. Corticosteroid injection gives ~3–4 months of functional benefit; worse baseline function predicts greater relief; radiographic severity predicts nothing.
  12. Hyaluronic acid: strong evidence of no benefit. PRP and stem cells: cannot be recommended.
  13. Anatomic TSA beats hemiarthroplasty (strong evidence). Anatomic vs reverse in a cuff-intact shoulder gives comparable outcomes, with aTSA better for rotation and rTSA possibly better for stiff shoulders.
  14. After anatomic TSA, protect the subscapularis. After reverse TSA, protect against extension with axial load and the internal rotation + adduction + extension dislocation position.
  15. Smoking and depression are the modifiable predictors of a worse surgical outcome — and both sit squarely in PM&R's scope before surgery.

Three things to carry out of this chapter about how good the evidence is:

The surgical evidence is far stronger than the non-surgical evidence. The AAOS guideline contains strong recommendations about implants and no recommendations at all about NSAIDs or corticosteroid injection — not because those don't work, but because nobody has run the trials. The physiotherapy guideline could issue only expert-opinion statements for non-operative care.

Almost all the comparative arthroplasty evidence is retrospective. The anatomic-versus-reverse systematic review found every included study was Oxford Level 3. Treat "aTSA gives better rotation" as a consistent observational finding, not a trial result.

Much of the pathophysiology is borrowed from the knee. The field's own 2025 consensus review says the post-traumatic and post-surgical pathways identified in knee OA still require validation in the shoulder. Hold the general mechanism confidently; hold the detail loosely.
